capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user
pull requests on the user's public repository

inputs.source: User's direct chat prompt in the desktop client
Issues opened by any GitHub user in the public repository, retrieved by the agent when it reviews open issues

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: 'The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private'; user prompt: 'Have a look at the open issues in my public repo.'
instructions.note: No system prompt or task-scoped credential restricts the agent to the public repository named in the request; the mounted PAT and available tools reach every private repository the user owns.

controls.name: Per-tool-call human approval prompt (arguments collapsed by default)
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a collapsed summary rather than the raw destination and payload, and approves many calls per session (approval fatigue). This is a model_summary gate: effectiveness decays under model upgrade (more persuasive, less alarming summaries), autonomy increase, and control removal.

controls.name: Scope the PAT to only the public repository needed for the task
controls.decay_rationale: A properly scoped credential does not decay with model capability; the model cannot read what the token cannot access.

controls.name: Pin the github-mcp-server image to a specific digest
controls.decay_rationale: Digest pinning does not decay with model capability; it prevents silent redefinition of tool behavior from an upstream image update (rug pull).

controls.name: Confirm PR destination bound to the system of record before create_pull_request executes
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced outside the model against the record of the intended repository, so it does not decay with model capability.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): a public issue can direct a private-repo read that is exfiltrated via a public pull request

attack_path.note: Untrusted content from any GitHub user opening an issue in the public repo enters the agent's context when it reviews open issues
Agent invokes get_file_contents against private repositories using a PAT with repo scope across all of the user's repos, public and private
Agent invokes create_pull_request on the public repo, placing retrieved private content into a PR visible to anyone, including the issue author

forecast.watch_signal: Rising approvals-per-session with collapsed arguments (approval fatigue), a client or model version change, or any change that removes or auto-approves the per-call prompt for this MCP server.

evidence.observation: "The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private."
"Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository."
"The client asks for approval per tool call. Arguments are collapsed by default. Users approve many calls per session."
Single github MCP server exposes both get_file_contents and create_pull_request under one GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN with no visible scoping.

recommendations.action: Issue a fine-grained PAT or GitHub App installation token scoped only to the public repository needed for the stated task; do not mount a token with private-repo scope into a session started to triage public issues.
Change the approval prompt to raw_action review: show the full destination repository, PR title, and diff contents before approval, rather than a collapsed summary.
Add a destination confirmation for create_pull_request bound to the system of record (the repo the user named), independent of model output.
Log and alert on any get_file_contents call against a private repo occurring in the same session as processing of an untrusted issue.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server image (SAFE-T1201 rug pull) can silently redefine tools used by a repo-wide credential

attack_path.note: MCP server image is pulled via docker run without a pinned tag or digest, so a session may run a different revision of the server code than the last one
A redefined tool could silently expand what get_file_contents does (e.g., add exfiltration of secrets) while keeping the same declared name and description
A redefined create_pull_request tool could add hidden side effects beyond what a collapsed approval summary discloses

forecast.watch_signal: The docker image digest actually pulled differs from the last recorded value, or the tools/list response (names, descriptions, schemas) changes without a corresponding config review.

evidence.observation: docker run args reference 'ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server' with no tag or digest, so 'docker run' resolves to whatever the mutable default currently points to
The same PAT with repo-wide scope is passed to this unpinned server on every invocation

recommendations.action: Pin the MCP server image to an immutable digest (docker run ... ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server@sha256:...) and review changes before updating.
Record and diff the tools/list response (names, descriptions, schemas) on every session start; alert on any change.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted public GitHub issue (U) can reach a repo-scoped read of private code and a public pull-request egress sink (S3) in two tool calls, the classic lethal trifecta (F1). A single PAT with repo scope across every owned repository, public and private, is mounted for a task the user scoped to the public repo only. The only declared control is a per-tool-call approval prompt; because arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, it is scored as a model_summary human approval gate (partially_dependent), which credits -2 tiers but is floored at moderate, giving a residual of moderate for F1. No structural control severs the path today: there is no least-privilege token scoping, no destination confirmation independent of model output, and the MCP server image is unpinned (F2). The forecast returns to critical under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or control_removal, any of which defeats the approval gate's already-limited effectiveness, and separately under new_mcp_server, where an unpinned upstream image update could silently redefine tool behavior behind the same weak approval gate.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration (the mcp.json and runtime notes provided), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt was provided; instruction-level findings are inferred from runtime notes and the user's request only, so confidence there is medium.
No verification was performed on the actual scopes granted to the PAT or the current digest of the github-mcp-server image; both are taken as declared, which limits confidence on F2 to low.
